newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore's Lee calls for China membership of WTO.
newsitem.headline: Singapore's Lee calls for China membership of WTO.

text.p: Singapore patriarch Lee Kuan Yew has called for China to be admitted to the World Trade Organisation (WTO) to help promote economic and political cooperation in Asia.

Lee said in a speech delivered in Washington and made available in Singapore on Tuesday that China should be given every incentive to choose international co-operation as it developed as a world power.

"This means China must have the economic opportunities to do this peacefully, without having to push its way to get resources like oil, and have access to markets for its goods and services," Lee said.
"China should be brought into the WTO after a short period of transition as a developing country. The world will not be better off with a China that is not bound by its rules.
"If such a route is not open to China, the world must live with a pushy China," he added.
The first ministerial meeting of the WTO, the global trade forum which succeeded the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), is due to be held in Singapore in December.

China was a founder member in 1948 of GATT but withdrew after the communist takeover in 1949. It has recently been pressing for WTO membership but has faced some opposition from Western diplomats who argue China should show more flexibility on a range of trade issues before being admitted.
Lee said he thought co-operation with China ought to be possible on a range of global political issues including nuclear proliferation, drug trafficking, global warming and terrorism.
He said a major source of instability in Asia would also be removed if China believed the United States was not helping Taiwan split away and declare separate independence.
Lee, Singapore prime minister for 31 years until 1990 and still in the cabinet as senior minister, is one of the few Asian statesmen able to boast close ties with Beijing, Taipei and Washington.
Turning to Hong Kong, Lee said China would do nothing intentionally to diminish Hong Kong's usefulness as an economic dynamo after it took over control from Britain on July 1, 1997.
"But there will be teething problems. With the best of goodwill on both sides it will be dificult to have a smooth transfer of power," he said.
